questions.stem: Two days after starting chemotherapy for leukemia, a client has a potassium of 6.4 mEq/L, a phosphorus of 7.2 mg/dL, a calcium of 7.0 mg/dL and a high uric acid. What does the nurse suspect?

rationale.correct: Tumor lysis syndrome: prevent it with aggressive hydration and allopurinol or rasburicase; monitor electrolytes and kidney function.

perOption.a: Rapid cell breakdown releases potassium, phosphorus and uric acid; phosphorus binds calcium.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
DRAFT: original question written with AI assistance; an RN or nurse educator must check it before candidates rely on it.

questions.stem: A client with lung cancer has swelling of the face and arms, distended neck veins and shortness of breath. What does the nurse suspect?

rationale.correct: SVC syndrome: keep the client upright, give oxygen and prepare for radiation or stenting.

perOption.a: A tumor blocks blood return from the upper body.
perOption.b: This isn't the best explanation with a mediastinal tumor.
perOption.d: This doesn't cause facial and arm swelling.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)

questions.stem: A client with metastatic prostate cancer reports new back pain and weakness in both legs. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Report it right away as a possible spinal cord compression
Give a heating pad and reassess tomorrow
Document it as expected bone pain

rationale.correct: Spinal cord compression: new back pain with neurologic changes is an emergency.

perOption.a: Early treatment (steroids, radiation) can prevent permanent paralysis.
perOption.d: The new weakness is a red flag.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
DRAFT: original question written with AI assistance; an RN or nurse educator must check it before candidates rely on it.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize spinal cord compression in cancer.

questions.stem: A client receiving chemotherapy has an ANC of 300/mm3 and a temperature of 38.4 °C (101.1 °F). What should the nurse do?

options.text: Notify the provider right away, draw blood cultures and expect broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour
Give acetaminophen and recheck in 4 hours

rationale.correct: Neutropenic fever (38.3 °C once, or 38.0 °C sustained, with ANC below 500): cultures and antibiotics within 1 hour.

perOption.a: Neutropenic fever is an emergency; sepsis can develop rapidly.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)

questions.stem: A client receiving chemotherapy has painful mouth sores. Which instruction should the nurse give?

options.text: Rinse with saline or baking soda solution and use a soft toothbrush
Eat spicy foods to stimulate appetite
Use a firm toothbrush to remove plaque

rationale.correct: Mucositis: gentle oral care, bland soft foods, avoid alcohol and tobacco, and use topical anesthetics as prescribed.

perOption.a: Gentle rinses clean the mouth and reduce irritation.
perOption.b: Alcohol dries and irritates the mucosa.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)

questions.stem: When should the nurse give a prescribed antiemetic to a client receiving highly emetogenic chemotherapy?

rationale.correct: Give antiemetics before chemotherapy and continue them as scheduled for delayed nausea.

perOption.a: Preventing nausea works better than treating it.
perOption.c: Some regimens continue for days, but the first dose is given before.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

questions.stem: A client is receiving doxorubicin. Which adverse effect is most important for the nurse to monitor?

rationale.correct: Doxorubicin: cardiotoxicity, myelosuppression and red urine (harmless); it is a vesicant.

perOption.a: Doxorubicin can cause dose-related heart failure; heart function is checked before and during treatment.
perOption.c: This is more typical of cisplatin.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

questions.stem: A client is receiving cisplatin. Which intervention helps prevent nephrotoxicity?

options.text: Vigorous IV hydration before and after the infusion

rationale.correct: Cisplatin: nephrotoxicity, ototoxicity, nausea and electrolyte loss.

perOption.a: Hydration dilutes cisplatin and protects the kidneys.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

questions.stem: A client receiving vincristine reports numbness and tingling in the fingers and constipation. What do these findings suggest?

rationale.correct: Vincristine: neuropathy and constipation; report worsening symptoms.

perOption.a: Vincristine causes peripheral neuropathy and autonomic effects such as constipation.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

questions.stem: A client receiving external beam radiation to the chest asks about skin care. Which statement shows a need for more teaching?

options.text: "I'll wash the area gently with lukewarm water and mild soap."
"I'll scrub off the ink markings when I shower."
"I'll protect the area from the sun."

rationale.correct: Radiation skin care: gentle washing, keep the markings, avoid lotions unless prescribed, and avoid sun, heat and cold.

perOption.a: This is appropriate.
perOption.b: The markings guide treatment and must not be removed.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)

questions.stem: A client starting chemotherapy is worried about hair loss. What is the best response?

options.text: "Hair loss is usually temporary. Let's talk about scarves, wigs or cutting your hair short beforehand."
"Don't worry, you won't lose your hair."
"Hair isn't important compared with your cancer."

rationale.correct: Alopecia affects body image; give accurate information and practical options.

perOption.a: This gives accurate information and supports coping.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)

questions.stem: After a left mastectomy with lymph node removal, which instruction should the nurse give?

options.text: "Don't allow blood pressures or blood draws on your left arm."
"Keep your left arm still for 6 months."
"Carry heavy bags on your left arm."

rationale.correct: After lymph node removal: protect the arm, do prescribed exercises and report swelling.

perOption.a: This reduces the risk of lymphedema and infection.
perOption.d: Lymphedema can often be prevented or managed.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)

questions.stem: A 42-year-old woman at average risk asks when she should have screening mammograms. What is the nurse's best response, based on current USPSTF guidance?

rationale.correct: Mammography every 2 years from 40 to 74 (USPSTF 2024); other organizations may advise annual screening.

perOption.a: USPSTF recommends biennial mammography from 40 to 74 for average-risk women.
perOption.c: Screening is for women without symptoms.

references: U.S. Preventive Services Task Force recommendations

questions.stem: When should a young man perform a testicular self-exam?

options.text: Once a year in a cold room

rationale.correct: Testicular self-exam: monthly after a warm shower; report painless lumps or heaviness.

perOption.a: Warmth relaxes the scrotum, making lumps easier to feel.
perOption.c: Testicular cancer is most common between 15 and 35.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old asks how often to have cervical cancer screening. What is the best response?

rationale.correct: Cervical screening: 21 to 29, Pap every 3 years; 30 to 65, HPV testing every 5 years or other approved options.

perOption.a: Ages 21 to 29: cytology every 3 years.
perOption.b: Annual screening isn't recommended for average risk.
perOption.d: Screening is for people without symptoms.

questions.stem: A client has newly diagnosed acute myeloid leukemia. Which nursing problem is the priority?

rationale.correct: Leukemia: infection and bleeding risks are the priorities.

perOption.a: Immature white cells don't fight infection, and infection is a leading cause of death.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)

questions.stem: Which finding is typical of Hodgkin lymphoma?

options.text: Painless, enlarged lymph node in the neck
Tender, red lymph node with sore throat

rationale.correct: Hodgkin lymphoma: painless lymph node swelling, sometimes with fever, night sweats and weight loss (B symptoms).

perOption.a: Painless lymphadenopathy is the classic presentation.
perOption.d: This suggests leukemia or low platelets.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)

questions.stem: A client with multiple myeloma has bone pain and a high calcium level. Which intervention is most important?

options.text: Encourage fluids of at least 2 to 3 L a day unless restricted

rationale.correct: Multiple myeloma: bone pain, fractures, hypercalcemia and kidney failure; hydration and fall safety are key.

perOption.a: Fluids help clear calcium and protect the kidneys from protein damage.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)

questions.stem: A client with cancer has constant pain. Which approach to pain relief is best?

options.text: Scheduled, around-the-clock analgesia with a breakthrough dose available
Medication only when pain is severe

rationale.correct: Cancer pain: around-the-clock dosing, breakthrough doses and preventing side effects such as constipation.

perOption.a: Steady levels prevent pain from returning, and breakthrough doses treat flares.
perOption.c: Opioids are appropriate for cancer pain.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

questions.stem: A dying client has noisy, gurgling breathing, and the family is upset. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Reposition the client on the side and give a prescribed anticholinergic

rationale.correct: Terminal secretions ('death rattle') are managed with positioning and anticholinergics such as glycopyrrolate, along with family support.

perOption.a: Positioning and drying secretions reduce the noise; explain that it's common near death.
perOption.b: Deep suctioning is distressing and usually not effective.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)

questions.stem: Which comfort measures should the nurse provide for a client who is actively dying? Select all that apply.

options.text: Pain and symptom medication as prescribed
Insisting the client eat full meals

rationale.correct: End-of-life care focuses on comfort, dignity and family support.

perOption.a: Mouth breathing dries the mucosa.
perOption.b: This prevents discomfort and skin breakdown.
perOption.d: This supports the client and family.
perOption.e: Appetite naturally falls; forcing food causes discomfort.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)

questions.stem: Which client is eligible for hospice care?

options.text: A client whose provider certifies a life expectancy of 6 months or less if the disease runs its usual course
A client who wants curative treatment
Only clients in the last week of life

rationale.correct: Hospice: prognosis of 6 months or less, focused on comfort.

perOption.a: This is the standard eligibility rule.
perOption.b: Eligibility depends on prognosis, not the diagnosis.
perOption.c: Hospice focuses on comfort rather than cure.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)

questions.stem: A client has just died, and no autopsy or coroner's case is involved. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Remove tubes and lines per policy, clean the body and let the family spend time with the client
Send the body to the morgue right away
Ask the family to leave while care is done, then send them home

rationale.correct: Postmortem care: follow policy, maintain dignity and support the family.

perOption.a: Postmortem care preserves dignity and supports grieving.
perOption.b: The family should have time with the client.
perOption.c: Tubes are left only for an autopsy or coroner's case.
perOption.d: The family may wish to stay or help.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)

questions.stem: A client will receive oral chemotherapy at home. Select the 3 safety instructions the nurse should give.

options.text: Wear gloves when handling the medication or body fluids
Flush the toilet twice after use
Crush tablets to make them easier to swallow
Let pregnant family members handle the pills
Store the medication with family members' medications

rationale.correct: Chemotherapy is hazardous; protect caregivers from exposure for about 48 hours after doses.

perOption.a: Chemotherapy is excreted in body fluids.
perOption.f: It should be stored separately and safely.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
